document.title: Taliban Structure and Leadership Chart
document.authors: National Security Archive (compiled from U.S. government sources)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
document.note: [Unclassified] Comprehensive chart compiled by the Archive entirely from U.S. government sources, giving biographical and professional information on more than 40 important Taliban officials.

key_claims: Mullah Omar was the final voice of authority in the Taliban and the main proponent of sheltering bin Ladin.
Rabbani, Omar's deputy until his death in April 2001, reportedly opposed Omar's protection of bin Ladin and wanted the issue settled.
Jalaluddin Haqqani was a military commander with a power base independent of Omar and close links to Arab and Kashmiri militants in Khost.
Haji Bashir Noorzai was a source of Taliban funding, reportedly from opium, and was close to Omar.
Abdul Jalil was the Taliban's conduit to Arab militants, and Muttawakil was reportedly tied to Pakistani intelligence.
Many senior Taliban figures began in Khalis's Hezb-i-Islami or Mohammadi's Harakat during the anti-Soviet jihad.
Omar reportedly demoted or purged officials blamed for failures, such as Ghaus after the 1997 Mazar-i-Sharif defeat.
Dadullah commanded Taliban frontline forces in the north and was implicated in abuses at Mazar-i-Sharif and Yakawlong.
Abdul Kabir ran the Taliban's eastern zone, controlled smuggling routes, and had strong links to Kabul and Pakistan.
Kabir had served under Jalaluddin Haqqani during the Soviet jihad and studied at Darul Uloom Haqqania.
Many Taliban leaders came from earlier mujahidin parties (Harakat, Ittehad-i-Islami, Hezb-i-Islami Khalis).
Abdul Wahab, a non-Kandahari close to Khalis, replaced Dilawar after the Saudi-Taliban dispute over bin Ladin.
Mullah Obaidullah, Minister of Defense, was Omar's military staffer and planned the Bamiyan Buddhas demolition.
Several officials (Rocketi, Khaksar) later defected, and others were killed or captured by U.S. or Pakistani forces.
